lessons.title: Ansible: inventory and ad-hoc commands
lessons.goal:
Learn how Ansible finds hosts (the inventory) and runs a single module on them, and see **idempotence** in action.

Why it matters: managing ten servers by SSH loops does not scale. Ansible describes the **desired state** and changes only what differs, over plain SSH, with no agent to install.

setup.note: Needs `ansible-core` (`dnf install ansible-core`). Everything runs against the local machine, so no remote hosts are needed; the commands are identical for remote hosts over SSH.

steps.title: How Ansible works
steps.text: Ansible runs on a **control node** (your laptop or a jump host). It reads an **inventory** (which hosts, in which groups), connects over **SSH**, copies a small Python program called a **module** to each host, runs it, and removes it. A module takes parameters, checks the current state, changes it only if needed, and reports `changed` or not. Nothing stays installed on the managed hosts except Python.

run.cmd: ansible --version | head -n 1 | sed 's/ \[core/ [core/'
export ANSIBLE_NOCOLOR=1 ANSIBLE_DEPRECATION_WARNINGS=False; echo 'colour and deprecation notices off for readable output'
run.output: colour and deprecation notices off for readable output

steps.title: The inventory
steps.text: An inventory is a file listing hosts in groups. Ours has one group, `local`, with one host that is reached **locally** (no SSH) so that the lesson works on a single machine. A real line looks like `web1.example.com ansible_user=deploy`.

run.cmd: cat inventory.ini

ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --list | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('groups:', sorted(g for g in d if g not in ('_meta','all'))); print('hosts in local:', d['local']['hosts'])"

steps.title: Ad-hoc: one module, one command
steps.text: `ansible HOSTS -m MODULE -a ARGS` runs a single module. `ping` checks that Ansible can connect and run Python (it is not ICMP). `command` runs a program.

run.cmd: ansible -i inventory.ini local -m ping -o | sed -E 's/\{.*\"ping\": \"pong\"\}/pong/' | cut -c1-80
ansible -i inventory.ini local -m command -a 'uname -s' -o | sed -E 's/.*\(stdout\)/(stdout)/' | cut -c1-60

steps.title: Idempotence
steps.text: The `file` module describes a **state** (`directory`), not an action ("make a directory"). The first run creates it and reports `changed: true`. The second run finds nothing to do and reports `changed: false`. Running the same description again and again is safe: that is **idempotence**.

run.cmd: ansible -i inventory.ini local -m file -a 'path=/tmp/lab/ansible-dir state=directory mode=0750' -o | grep -oE 'CHANGED|SUCCESS|"changed": (true|false)' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
ansible -i inventory.ini local -m file -a 'path=/tmp/lab/ansible-dir state=directory mode=0750' -o | grep -oE 'CHANGED|SUCCESS|"changed": (true|false)' | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.after: First run: `CHANGED`, `changed: true`. Second: `SUCCESS`, `changed: false`. Compare with `mkdir`, which fails on the second run.

steps.title: Modules for everything
steps.text: There are modules for files (`copy`, `file`, `lineinfile`, `template`), packages (`dnf`, `apt`), services (`systemd`), users (`user`), commands (`command`, `shell`) and thousands more. `ansible-doc MODULE` shows the parameters.

run.cmd: ansible-doc -l 2>/dev/null | grep -cE '^ansible.builtin' | awk '{print $1, "built-in modules"}'
ansible-doc ansible.builtin.lineinfile 2>/dev/null | sed -n '/^> /p;/^  Manage lines/p' | head -n 2 | sed 's/ (.*//'

steps.under: Ansible's SSH usage is **agentless**: for each task it opens (or reuses, with `ControlPersist`) an SSH connection, uploads the module to a temporary directory, runs it, reads JSON back and deletes it. That makes it easy to start but slower per task than agent-based tools; `pipelining` and `forks` speed it up. Use `command`/`shell` modules only when no specific module exists, because they cannot know whether anything changed.

quiz.q: What does Ansible install on managed hosts?
options: Nothing permanent: modules are copied, run and removed
Applying the same description repeatedly yields the same state, changing nothing the second time
That Ansible can connect and run Python on the hosts
quiz.explain: It is an Ansible module, not ICMP.

quiz.q: Where are hosts and groups defined?
quiz.explain: The inventory file or dynamic inventory.

check.scenario: You must make sure `chronyd` is installed, enabled and running on 50 servers, today and again next month. Show the ad-hoc commands and explain why they are safe to repeat.
check.answer: `ansible all -b -m ansible.builtin.dnf -a 'name=chrony state=present'` and `ansible all -b -m ansible.builtin.systemd -a 'name=chronyd state=started enabled=yes'` (`-b` = become root). Each module describes a state, so hosts that already comply report `ok` and nothing changes; only drifted hosts change. In practice put them in a playbook under version control.

lessons.title: Playbooks: tasks, variables, handlers and check mode
lessons.goal:
Write a playbook that describes a small configuration, run it twice to see idempotence, change a variable to trigger a **handler**, and preview changes with `--check --diff`.

Why it matters: playbooks are your servers' configuration as code: reviewable, repeatable and testable, the opposite of hand-edited machines.

setup.note: Needs `ansible-core` (`dnf install ansible-core`). Everything runs against the local machine, so no remote hosts are needed; the commands are identical for remote hosts over SSH.

steps.title: A playbook
steps.text: A playbook is a YAML list of **plays**. A play targets `hosts`, may set `vars`, and lists **tasks**; each task calls one module with parameters. **Handlers** run only when notified by a task that **changed** something, once, at the end. `{{ motd_text }}` is a Jinja2 variable.

code.src:
- name: Configure a lab host
  hosts: local
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    motd_text: "Managed by Ansible"
  tasks:
    - name: Create the application directory
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /tmp/lab/app
        state: directory
        mode: "0755"

    - name: Write the configuration file
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: /tmp/lab/app/app.conf
        content: |
          port=8080
          motd={{ motd_text }}
      notify: reload app

    - name: Make sure debug is off
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /tmp/lab/app/app.conf
        line: "debug=false"

  handlers:
    - name: reload app
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "the application would be reloaded now"

run.cmd: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --syntax-check 2>&1 | sed 's/^playbook: //'

run.cmd: printf '[local]\nlocalhost ansible_connection=local ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3\n' > inventory.ini; cat inventory.ini | head -n 1

steps.title: First run: three changes and a handler
steps.text: Everything is new, so all three tasks report `changed` and the handler runs at the end. `PLAY RECAP` summarises per host.

run.cmd: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml 2>&1 | grep -vE '^$'
run.output:
PLAY [Configure a lab host] ****************************************************
TASK [Create the application directory] ****************************************
changed: [localhost]
TASK [Write the configuration file] ********************************************
changed: [localhost]
TASK [Make sure debug is off] **************************************************
changed: [localhost]
RUNNING HANDLER [reload app] ***************************************************
ok: [localhost] => {
    "msg": "the application would be reloaded now"
}
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
localhost                  : ok=4    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

steps.after: The task that wrote the file **notified** the handler, which ran once after all tasks.

steps.title: Second run: nothing to do
steps.text: Running the same playbook again changes nothing: `changed=0`, and the handler does **not** run.

run.cmd: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml 2>&1 | grep -E 'changed=|RUNNING HANDLER' | sed -E 's/  +/ /g'
run.output:
RUNNING HANDLER [reload app] ***************************************************
localhost : ok=4 changed=2 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0

run.cmd: cat app/app.conf

steps.title: Change a variable: only what differs changes
steps.text: `-e motd_text=Hello` overrides the variable. Only the task that uses it changes, and the handler fires again.

run.cmd: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml -e motd_text=Hello 2>&1 | grep -E '^(changed|ok):|RUNNING HANDLER|changed=' | sed -E 's/  +/ /g'
run.output:
ok: [localhost]
changed: [localhost]
changed: [localhost]
RUNNING HANDLER [reload app] ***************************************************
ok: [localhost] => {
localhost : ok=4 changed=2 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0

run.cmd: cat app/app.conf | head -n 2

steps.title: Check mode and diff: look before you leap
steps.text: `--check` is a dry run: modules report what **would** change without changing anything. `--diff` shows the file differences. Use both before running on production.

run.cmd: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml -e motd_text=Planned --check --diff 2>&1 | grep -E '^(---|\+\+\+|[-+]motd)|changed=' | sed -E 's#/tmp/lab/app/##; s/  +/ /g'
run.output:
--- before: app.conf
+++ after: /home/opc/.ansible/tmp/ansible-local-394297zy7chtmr/tmpxg4uz6y7
-motd=Hello
+motd=Planned
localhost : ok=4 changed=1 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0

run.cmd: cat app/app.conf | head -n 2

steps.under: A playbook is executed task by task, on all hosts of the play in parallel batches (`forks`, default 5). For each host and task Ansible sends the module, gets the result, and decides the next step. Reusable pieces are packaged as **roles** (a directory structure of tasks, templates, defaults and handlers) and shared through collections. Secrets belong in **Ansible Vault**, not in the playbook.

options: Once at the end of the play, if a notifying task reported a change
Shows what would change, with file differences, without changing anything

quiz.q: A second run of an idempotent playbook shows `changed=3`. What does that suggest?
options: Some task is not idempotent (for example a command task) or something keeps changing
quiz.explain: A good playbook reports changed=0 when nothing drifted.

quiz.q: Where should passwords in playbooks be stored?

check.scenario: A playbook that uses `ansible.builtin.shell: echo 'port=80' >> /etc/app.conf` shows `changed` on every run and the file keeps growing. How do you fix it?
check.answer: Use a state-based module: `ansible.builtin.lineinfile: path=/etc/app.conf line='port=80'` (adds the line once), or `copy`/`template` for the whole file. If a command must be used, make it idempotent with `creates:`/`removes:` or `changed_when:` so Ansible can tell whether anything changed.

interview.q: What is Ansible and why is it called agentless?
interview.a: A configuration management and automation tool that connects over SSH, runs modules and removes them; no daemon on managed hosts. See [the lesson](#/lesson/47/ansible-adhoc-inventory).

interview.q: What is idempotence and why does it matter?
interview.a: Applying the same configuration repeatedly gives the same result and changes nothing after the first run, so playbooks are safe to re-run and to use for drift correction.

Tasks triggered by `notify` that run once at the end of the play only if a notifying task changed something (typically restarting or reloading a service). See [the lesson](#/lesson/47/ansible-playbooks).

interview.q: How do you preview changes safely?
interview.a: `ansible-playbook --check --diff` (dry run with file diffs), plus `--limit` to a test host first.

interview.q: What is the difference between command/shell and specific modules?
interview.a: Specific modules describe state and are idempotent; command/shell run arbitrary commands and cannot know if anything changed unless you add creates/changed_when.
A reusable directory structure (tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, files, meta) that packages related configuration so it can be shared and versioned.

glossary.def: An agentless automation tool that applies desired state over SSH.
The list of managed hosts and groups.
A unit of work (file, dnf, systemd...) that Ansible runs on a host.
Re-running yields the same state and no changes after the first run.
A YAML file describing plays: hosts, variables, tasks and handlers.
A task that runs at the end of a play when notified by a changed task.
A reusable packaging of tasks, templates and defaults.
